first_touch.label: First Touch
first_touch.looks_for: What happens in the half-second the ball arrives — does it stick, or does it bounce away? It is the fastest honesty test in football.

scale.6: The ball obeys when there's time and space.
scale.8: The ball is tamed even with a defender breathing down the neck — rare at youth level.
scale.9: The first touch already IS the next move — pro academies build around this.

low: {name} is still making friends with the ball — and that friendship is exactly what training fixes fastest.
Every great first touch started as a bouncy one. This is the most trainable number in the whole report.
mid: When {name} gets a clean moment, the ball settles like it wants to stay.
The next discovery: keeping that calm touch when someone is chasing — that's what turns heads.
high: The ball arrives and simply… stops. Most {age}-year-olds need two touches for what {name} does in one.
This is the kind of touch academy coaches remember on the drive home.

first_touch.next_level: At academy level, a first touch isn't about control — it's about direction. The touch becomes the first pass.

ball_control.label: Ball Control
ball_control.looks_for: Can the ball live close to the feet at speed, in crowds, on bad grass? Control is what makes every other skill possible.

scale.6: Comfortable in open play, loses it in traffic.
scale.8: The ball stays close even in crowded moments — defenders have to foul to get it.
scale.9: The ball looks glued — elite academies treat this as a signature trait.

low: The ball still escapes {name} in tight moments — which means there's a whole level waiting to be unlocked with daily touches.
Ten minutes of ball mastery a day rewrites this number faster than any other.
mid: {name} keeps the ball close enough to be trusted with it — teammates notice that long before anyone else does.
The next step is making the ball feel small in BIG moments.
high: Watch {name}'s feet in traffic: the ball stays inside a shoebox. That's not luck — that's thousands of touches showing up.
See control like this and you stop watching the ball — you start watching the player.

ball_control.next_level: The next level asks for control at full sprint — same closeness, twice the speed.

dribbling.label: Dribbling
dribbling.looks_for: Not tricks — bravery with a plan. Does the player attack a defender on purpose, and does the move actually gain ground?

scale.6: Dribbles when there's space to invite it.
scale.8: Takes players on by choice and wins more duels than he loses — academy coaches underline this.
scale.9: Beats his man both ways and the defence has to plan for it.

low: {name} still passes the responsibility away in 1v1s — courage grows every time a coach says 'try again'.
Dribbling is a permission skill: once {name} is told mistakes are welcome, this number moves.
mid: {name} dares — and daring is the half of dribbling that can't be taught.
Now it's about picking the moment: the best dribblers say no as often as they say go.
high: {name} runs AT defenders — on purpose. Most kids this age run away from that moment; {name} invites it.
That bravery is the loudest line in any match report.

dribbling.next_level: Higher up, dribbling becomes economics: beat your man AND keep the team's shape alive.

passing.label: Passing
passing.looks_for: Weight, timing and choice — can he keep the ball moving under pressure, and does the pass make the receiver's life easier?

scale.6: Safe, sideways, keeps things ticking when unpressured.
scale.8: Finds a teammate even with a defender closing in — most players this age just clear it.
scale.9: Breaks lines and flips the pitch — the pass academies are built on.

low: {name}'s passes still panic under pressure — which simply means the eyes and feet aren't synced YET.
This is where wall-passes and rondos quietly build a new player.
mid: {name} keeps teammates in the game — the pass arrives where it should, when it should.
The discovery ahead: passes that don't just keep the ball, but hurt the opponent.
high: {name} finds a teammate under pressure — something most {age}-year-olds simply cannot do yet.
A pass like this sends a message: the head is faster than the game.

passing.next_level: The next tier plays forward first: same accuracy, braver direction.

shooting.label: Shooting
shooting.looks_for: Clean strike, quick release, and the calm to pick a corner instead of just kicking hard.

scale.6: Strikes well when the ball is set and there's time.
scale.8: Gets shots off fast in real game chaos and tests the keeper — that's finishing, not just shooting.
scale.9: Chooses placement over power under pressure — elite instinct.

low: {name}'s strike is still more enthusiasm than technique — the fun part is that technique is 100% buildable.
A hundred repetitions of the same clean strike will change this number and {name}'s confidence with it.
mid: {name} hits the target more often than not — keepers have to work.
The next unlock is speed: half a second faster from chance to shot changes everything.
high: When a chance appears, {name} is already shooting while others are still deciding.
Coaches call this 'the trigger' — you either build it young or chase it forever.

shooting.next_level: Higher levels shrink time: the same finish with half the backswing and no second invitation.

weak_foot.label: Weak Foot
weak_foot.looks_for: Not equality — usability. Can the weak foot pass, receive and finish well enough that defenders can't just show him one way?

scale.6: Emergency use only — defenders can steer him.
scale.8: Genuinely two-sided in passes and touches — doubles his options on the pitch.
scale.9: Defenders can't plan against him — both feet threaten.

low: Right now defenders have a map of {name}: force the weak side. The great news — this is the cheapest superpower in football to build.
Ten minutes a day against a wall, and in six months this becomes a different report.
mid: {name}'s weak foot is no longer a secret weakness — it does honest work.
Full trust in it under pressure is the last door to open.
high: Two working feet at {age} turn heads instantly: it means every drill ever done counted twice.
Defenders lose their favourite trick against {name} — there is no weak side to push him onto.

weak_foot.next_level: At academy level the weak foot isn't tested in drills — it's tested with a defender arriving. That's the standard.

one_v_one.label: 1v1 Duels
one_v_one.looks_for: The moment football gets personal: does he win his direct duels — with skill, timing or pure will?

scale.6: Competes but usually needs help.
scale.8: Wins most of his direct battles — teammates start giving him the ball on purpose.
scale.9: A duel-winner both ways — attack and defence. Academies track this number hard.

low: {name} still loses more duels than he wins — every lost duel at {age} is a free lesson nobody has to pay for.
Duels are won in training courage first, matches second.
mid: {name} holds his own when the game gets personal — that earns respect fast, on both teams.
The next discovery: winning duels on purpose, not just on effort.
high: When it becomes one against one, {name} usually walks away with the ball — that's a trait, not a coincidence.
Duel-winners get remembered, because duels are the moments everyone watches.

one_v_one.next_level: Next level up, everyone is fast and strong — duels are won with body position and timing instead.

positioning.label: Positioning
positioning.looks_for: Where is he standing when he DOESN'T have the ball? Good positioning is invisible to most parents — and glowing to a trained eye.

scale.6: Follows the ball like most kids — heart over map.
scale.8: Repeatedly in the right zone before the ball arrives — plays the game in advance.
scale.9: Organises space for others too — a coach on the pitch.

low: {name} still chases the ball like it owes him money — normal at {age}, and exactly what game-understanding training fixes.
The magic phrase is 'where SHOULD you be?' — asked a hundred times, it becomes instinct.
mid: {name} is starting to appear in the right places before the ball does — the first sign of a thinking footballer.
This is the quiet skill that makes coaches trust a player with minutes.
high: {name} is already standing where the game is going to happen — that's not running, that's reading.
Academy coaches flag this early because it's the hardest thing to teach late.

positioning.next_level: At higher levels positioning is measured every 5 seconds, not every attack — constant small corrections.

off_ball_movement.label: Off-Ball Movement
off_ball_movement.looks_for: Runs that create space — for himself AND for teammates. The players who move without reward today get picked tomorrow.

scale.6: Moves when called, waits when not.
scale.8: Makes runs that drag defenders and open doors — even when he never gets the pass.
scale.9: His movement is a weapon the whole team plays off.

low: When the ball leaves {name}, he switches off — turning those seconds ON is one of the fastest visible upgrades in football.
The players who move without the ball get it twice as often. That's the whole secret.
mid: {name} keeps playing when the ball is elsewhere — runs that quietly stretch the game.
The next unlock is timing: same run, two seconds later, completely different result.
high: {name} plays 90% of the game without the ball — and wins that 90%.
Runs that never get rewarded still get noticed. The trained eye writes those down.

off_ball_movement.next_level: The next level rewards double movement — the fake run that frees the real one.

scanning.label: Scanning
scanning.looks_for: Shoulder checks before the ball arrives. It's the clearest window into how fast a young brain is playing the game.

scale.6: Looks after receiving — decisions come late.
scale.8: Checks his shoulder before the ball arrives — he's playing 2 seconds ahead of everyone.
scale.9: Scans constantly and plays what he saw — the trademark of academy midfielders.

low: {name} receives the ball and THEN starts looking — flip that order and a completely different player appears.
Two shoulder checks before every touch. Small habit. Massive discovery.
mid: {name} is starting to look before the ball comes — the game is slowing down for him.
When scanning becomes automatic, everything else in this report gets easier.
high: {name} already knows what's behind him before the ball arrives — he's playing in the future while others react in the present.
Ask any academy coach what they look for first in midfielders. This. This exact thing.

scanning.next_level: The next level scans under sprint and contact — same eyes, hostile conditions.

decision_making.label: Decision Making
decision_making.looks_for: Pass, dribble or shoot — and was it the RIGHT one? Slow legs get forgiven long before slow choices do.

scale.6: Decides late; the good option often expires.
scale.8: Picks the right option under pressure more often than not — that's football IQ showing.
scale.9: Makes hard choices look obvious — the game bends to his tempo.

low: {name} has the tools but hesitates on which one to use — decisions are a muscle, and it grows with every game watched and played.
The question that builds this: 'what did you see?' — after every single action.
mid: {name} usually chooses well — the ball tends to leave him in a better place than it arrived.
The next level of this is speed: same good choice, one second sooner.
high: {name} makes the right call while the game is screaming at him — composure like this at {age} is what separates players.
Feet can be trained. Brains get queued for.

decision_making.next_level: Higher up, there is no time to decide — the decision must be made before the ball arrives.

timing_of_runs.label: Timing of Runs
timing_of_runs.looks_for: Not how fast the run is — WHEN it starts. A perfectly timed run beats a fast one every time.

scale.6: Runs early and gets caught offside, or late and misses it.
scale.8: Arrives exactly as the ball does — the kind of timing that creates goals from nothing.
scale.9: Times runs off the passer's body shape — practically telepathy.

low: {name}'s runs and the passes don't speak the same language yet — timing comes from repetitions with the same teammates.
One tip changes this: start the run when the passer's head comes UP.
mid: {name}'s runs are starting to sync with the game's rhythm — arriving with the ball instead of after it.
This skill quietly turns average teams into dangerous ones.
high: {name} arrives at the exact second the ball does — that's not speed, that's a clock in his head.
Perfectly timed runs are the moments people rewind the video for. Literally.

timing_of_runs.next_level: The next level times runs against the offside line — a game of centimetres and half-seconds.

game_understanding.label: Game Understanding
game_understanding.looks_for: Does he understand WHY things happen — momentum, space, danger — or is he just reacting to the ball?

scale.6: Understands his own job in the moment.
scale.8: Reads the WHOLE game — presses at the right time, slows it when the team needs air.
scale.9: Sees the game like a coach — rare and priceless at youth level.

low: {name} plays the moment, not yet the story of the game — watching football WITH questions is the fastest teacher.
Ten minutes of match analysis together beats an hour of cones for this number.
mid: {name} is starting to sense the game's temperature — when to hurry, when to breathe.
This is the number that quietly predicts how far the rest can travel.
high: {name} understands the game's WHY — pressing at the right moment, calming it when the team needs air. Coaches build teams around brains like this.
Legs sell tickets. Understanding wins careers.

game_understanding.next_level: At the next level this becomes leadership — seeing it is step one, organising others around it is step two.

acceleration.label: Acceleration
acceleration.looks_for: The first 5 metres — football's most valuable distance. Most duels are decided before top speed even matters.

scale.6: Average burst — wins some, loses some.
scale.8: First 3 steps win him separations others need 10 metres for.
scale.9: Explosive first metres that change what positions he can play.

low: {name}'s first steps are still gears, not a spring — and spring can absolutely be trained at {age}.
Short hill sprints and skipping work: boring, cheap, and they rewrite this number.
mid: {name} gets away cleanly when he decides early — burst and brain are starting to cooperate.
The next level: exploding on the FIRST step, not the third.
high: {name}'s first three steps are a getaway car — by the time defenders react, the moment is over.
The first 5 metres get measured, not the 50. {name} wins the ones that matter.

acceleration.next_level: Higher up, acceleration is used tactically — saved, disguised and released at the perfect moment.

speed.label: Speed
speed.looks_for: Real game speed — WITH the ball, under pressure, in the final minutes. Track speed is nice; football speed wins matches.

scale.6: Keeps up with the game.
scale.8: Faster than the game — and crucially, nearly as fast WITH the ball.
scale.9: A separation weapon defences must plan entire shapes around.

low: {name} isn't winning foot-races yet — but growth spurts rewrite this page more than any other. Patience is a strategy here.
Meanwhile: players who think fast never look slow.
mid: {name} has honest pace — enough to punish hesitation.
The real discovery is keeping that pace with the ball attached.
high: {name} moves at a speed that forces opponents to change their plan — that's not a stat, that's leverage.
And the rarest part: the ball doesn't slow him down much.

speed.next_level: At the next level everyone is fast — the edge becomes speed WITH control and AFTER 60 minutes.

balance.label: Balance
balance.looks_for: Staying playable through contact and sharp turns. Balance is why some players bounce off challenges that flatten others.

scale.6: Stable until contact arrives.
scale.8: Rides bumps and stays on his feet with the ball — referees stop mattering.
scale.9: Contact barely registers — plays through fouls.

low: {name} still goes down easier than he should — core work and single-leg play quietly fix this in months.
Balance is the least glamorous superpower and one of the most trainable.
mid: {name} stays on his feet when it gets physical — a quiet advantage every single match.
The next unlock: using balance to shield and turn, not just survive.
high: Defenders bump {name} and he simply… continues. Balance like this makes every other skill usable under fire.
It can't be faked on video — which is exactly why it counts.

balance.next_level: The next level weaponises balance — shielding, rolling off contact, drawing fouls on purpose.

agility.label: Agility
agility.looks_for: Direction changes at speed — the tight-space wiggle that makes defenders look like they're moving in slow motion.

scale.6: Turns need a moment of setup.
scale.8: Changes direction sharply enough to lose markers in phone-booth spaces.
scale.9: Twists through gaps that don't officially exist.

low: {name} still turns like a bus in tight spaces — ladder and cone work make this one of the fastest numbers to move.
Every sharp turn trained now is a defender lost later.
mid: {name} can lose a marker in a small space when it matters.
Next: doing it at full speed without the touch suffering.
high: {name} changes direction like the pitch has trapdoors — defenders commit and he's already gone.
In small-sided football, this is the skill that makes highlight reels.

agility.next_level: The next level pairs agility with deception — the shoulder drop that sells the wrong direction first.

intensity.label: Intensity
intensity.looks_for: Does the effort survive the whole video? The trained eye fast-forwards to the last minutes on purpose.

scale.6: Bright starts, quiet finishes.
scale.8: Same hunger in minute 1 and minute 50 — the engine coaches trust.
scale.9: Sets the intensity for everyone else — a standard-carrier.

low: {name}'s effort comes in waves right now — engines are built, not born, and {age} is exactly when they get built.
The habit that changes this: sprint back the moment the ball is lost. Every time.
mid: {name} keeps working long after the cameras usually stop caring — that consistency is currency.
The last minutes of a video get watched on purpose. {name} survives the fast-forward.
high: Minute one and minute fifty look identical for {name} — that engine is a decision he makes, not a gift he got.
Talent opens doors. Engines keep them open.

intensity.next_level: At the next level intensity is managed, not just spent — max effort in the right 20 moments.

body_control.label: Body Control
body_control.looks_for: Coordination in awkward moments — bouncing balls, bad passes, mid-air adjustments. The clumsy-ball test.

scale.6: Comfortable with clean service only.
scale.8: Tames bad passes and bouncing balls — makes messy football look tidy.
scale.9: Adjusts mid-air, mid-stride, mid-chaos — athlete's genes plus training.

low: Awkward balls still beat {name} — juggling ugly (bounces, thighs, shoulders) is the playful fix.
Coordination trains best before 14. The window is wide open.
mid: {name} handles football's messy moments — bad bounces don't break his play.
The next level: making an awkward ball into an ADVANTAGE.
high: Bad pass, weird bounce, ball in the air — {name}'s body just solves it. That's coordination you can't choreograph.
Coaches notice players who make messy football look calm.

body_control.next_level: Higher levels serve almost no perfect balls — body control becomes a starting requirement.

confidence.label: Confidence
confidence.looks_for: Does he WANT the ball — especially right after a mistake? Confidence shows in the hands that go up asking for it.

scale.6: Confident when things go well.
scale.8: Demands the ball even under pressure, even after errors — that's real, not loud.
scale.9: His confidence lifts the whole team's — a presence.

low: {name} hides a little when the game gets loud — confidence is built from small wins, and this report is a map of them.
Show {name} his own best moments from this video. Watch what happens.
mid: {name} wants the ball more often than he avoids it — the scale is tipping the right way.
The breakthrough moment: asking for the ball 10 seconds after losing it.
high: {name} wants the ball even when the game is on fire — courage like this can't be coached into a player, only coached OUT by mistake.
Protect this. It's worth more than any single skill on this page.

confidence.next_level: At the next level everyone gets humbled weekly — confidence must be rebuilt every Monday. That's the skill.

work_rate.label: Work Rate
work_rate.looks_for: The runs nobody claps for — tracking back, closing down, going again. Effort is the first thing video can verify and the last thing anyone forgives.

scale.6: Works when the game rewards it.
scale.8: Presses, tracks and repeats — with or without applause.
scale.9: Outworks everyone as identity, not mood.

low: {name} saves his legs for the fun moments — flipping that is free talent lying on the ground.
Work rate is the only number in this report {name} fully controls tomorrow morning.
mid: {name} does the unglamorous running that wins coaches over.
Next: making it constant — effort as identity, not as reaction.
high: {name} runs for the team when nobody's watching — the trained eye ALWAYS watches for exactly that.
Skill decides if you're interesting. Work rate decides if you stay.

work_rate.next_level: The next level measures work rate in numbers — distance, sprints, presses. It becomes a stat, not an opinion.

courage_in_duels.label: Courage in Duels
courage_in_duels.looks_for: The 50/50 test: does he go in honestly, or does he pull out at the last step? You can see character in one tackle.

scale.6: Picks his battles carefully.
scale.8: Goes into 50/50s like they're 70/30 — bravery with technique.
scale.9: The player others hide behind when the game turns nasty.

low: {name} still steps back from the crunch moments — courage grows with padding drills and permission to fail.
Nobody expects a fearless {age}-year-old. What matters is the direction of travel.
mid: {name} goes into contact honestly — no half-measures that cause injuries.
The next level: ARRIVING first, because first usually wins.
high: When it's 50/50, {name} makes it 70/30 with pure intent — that mentality is contagious in a good team.
Bravery gets noted in the margins because it never shows in stats.

courage_in_duels.next_level: Higher up, duels are chess — courage stays, recklessness gets trained out.

response_to_mistakes.label: Response to Mistakes
response_to_mistakes.looks_for: The 10 seconds AFTER a bad touch. Head up or head down? You learn more from errors than from goals.

scale.6: Mistakes cost a few minutes of good football.
scale.8: Bounces back within seconds — hunts the ball to fix it himself.
scale.9: Uses mistakes as fuel — visibly plays BETTER after errors.

low: A mistake still switches {name} off for a while — the 5-second rule (sprint to win it back) is the antidote, and it works.
Every player on TV was once a kid whose head dropped. The ones who made it learned this exact skill.
mid: {name} recovers from errors faster than most — the game doesn't lose him for long.
The final step: treating the mistake as the START of the next action.
high: {name} answers his own mistakes within seconds — winning the ball back like it's personal. This gets CIRCLED in the notes.
This is the single strongest predictor of surviving academy football.

response_to_mistakes.next_level: At the next level mistakes are public — crowds, coaches, cameras. The bounce-back must be armour-plated by then.

competitive_mindset.label: Competitive Mindset
competitive_mindset.looks_for: Does losing bother him — in the right way? The fire that hates losing but keeps its head.

scale.6: Competes while it's fun.
scale.8: Hates losing productively — fights to the whistle without losing control.
scale.9: Drags teammates into battles they'd given up on.

low: {name} plays for joy more than for victory right now — and honestly, at {age}, joy is the fuel that lasts longest.
Competitive fire usually arrives with the teenage years. Watch this space.
mid: {name} clearly minds losing — and channels it into playing, not sulking.
That balance between fire and control is exactly what coaches search for.
high: {name} competes like the result is personal — every duel, every restart, to the final whistle.
You can teach tactics to a competitor. You can't teach competing to a passenger.

competitive_mindset.next_level: The next level tests the fire weekly against equals — staying hungry when winning stops being easy.

focus.label: Focus
focus.looks_for: Concentration when the ball is far away — the marking, the line, the small jobs. Switching off for 5 seconds is how goals are conceded.

scale.6: Locked in when involved, drifts when not.
scale.8: Stays switched on through the boring minutes — rare and quietly elite at youth level.
scale.9: Ninety-minute concentration — reads danger before it forms.

low: {name}'s mind wanders when the ball does — normal at {age}, and trainable with small jobs ('own the offside line for 10 minutes').
Focus is a muscle. Short reps, growing sets.
mid: {name} stays in the game even when the game isn't with him.
The next level: focus that TALKS — warning teammates before danger arrives.
high: {name} concentrates through the quiet minutes where most kids mentally leave the pitch — the next level tests exactly this, off the ball.
Boring-minute focus is what separates 'talented' from 'reliable'. {name} has it.

focus.next_level: At the next level a 5-second nap costs a goal — focus becomes a professional requirement, not a bonus.

Goalkeeper.line: Watch a young keeper's feet and voice before his hands — shot-stopping is assumed at the next level; the rest is what gets measured.

weighs.why: A metre of good positioning saves more shots than a metre of diving ever will.
Keepers live alone with their mistakes — confidence decides if one error becomes three.
Come or stay, catch or punch, short or long — a keeper makes more decisions than anyone.

Centre-back.line: For a centre-back, reading the game weighs above everything — the best defenders defend with their brain first.

weighs.why: Great centre-backs intercept quietly; poor ones tackle heroically. The trained eye prefers quiet.
The box is a battlefield — hesitation at centre-back is visible from the stands.
Modern academies demand defenders who START attacks, not just stop them.

alt.why: Eyes and passing range like this often grow best one line higher, where turning the game matters more than recovery pace.

Full-back.line: Full-back is football's double shift — engine and 1v1 defending weigh first, delivery second.

weighs.why: The position runs both boxes all game — no engine, no full-back.
A full-back is left alone with a winger 30 times per match. Survival is the job.
The overlap only works if it arrives at the exact right second.

alt.why: When a full-back's attacking numbers outshine his defending ones, coaches often push him 20 metres forward — the same run, but ending in the box.

Wing-back.line: Wing-backs are measured as athletes first — the position covers more grass than any other on the pitch.

weighs.why: Wing-back without a monster engine isn't a position, it's a liability.
The whole flank is his — recovering AND attacking it demands real pace.
Alone on the touchline: cross, cut back, recycle or defend — 50 lonely choices a game.

Defensive Midfielder.line: The 6 is measured by brain-speed: scanning and positioning weigh double here, because everything happens around him.

weighs.why: The 6 receives with opponents on his back all game — no scanning, no position.
He is the shield. One step wrong and the whole defence is exposed.
Every attack starts through him — his pass sets the team's tempo.

alt.why: Duel-winning plus ball-carrying suggests he can play higher, where breaking lines himself becomes a weapon instead of a risk.

Central Midfielder.line: Central midfield is the thinking position — scanning and decisions weigh above athleticism here.

weighs.why: The middle is 360° chaos — midfielders live or die by what they see before receiving.
He touches the ball more than anyone; each touch is a decision the team inherits.
A midfielder's pass is his voice — range and weight decide how much he can say.

alt.why: A midfielder who arrives and finishes like this may be wasted starting deep — the numbers point ten metres forward.

Attacking Midfielder.line: The 10 is measured on moments: decision-making and the final pass weigh heaviest — creating what wasn't there.

weighs.why: The 10 gets the ball where mistakes are cheap and magic is expensive — choices define him.
He receives between the lines with his back to goal — the touch must buy him time that isn't there.
Great 10s appear in pockets no one else sees — movement IS the creativity.

alt.why: Engine and discipline above flair suggests a future as a box-to-box 8 — more touches, more influence, same attacking moments.

Winger.line: Wingers are measured on bravery first: 1v1 numbers weigh heaviest, then what he chooses the second he's past his man.

weighs.why: The winger's whole job description is written in duels — beat your man or the position doesn't exist.
The first three steps decide whether the 1v1 even happens.
Beating the man is half the job — the cross, cut-back or shot afterwards is the paycheck.

alt.why: Eyes and passing ahead of raw burst is a midfielder's profile — central areas reward what he's already best at.
Wingers who love the box more than the byline often become strikers — the finishing instinct is the rare part.

Striker.line: Strikers are measured backwards — from the finish. Timing and the shot trigger weigh above build-up play.

weighs.why: Goals are scored before the ball is kicked — with a run started half a second earlier than the defender's.
One touch, one strike — the striker's economy is measured in half-chances converted.
Strikers miss more than they score. The next chance belongs to the ones who forget instantly.

alt.why: A striker who creates as naturally as he finishes might influence the game more facing it than backing into it.
